summary: This document specifies use of Bidirectional Forwarding Detection in RBridge campuses, based on the RBridge Channel extension to TRILL. BFD is a widely deployed OAM mechanism in IP and MPLS networks.

eli5.summary: Two neighbors keep waving to show they are still there. This lets TRILL switches do the same so a failure is noticed quickly.

questions: how does trill detect neighbor failure
subtitle: How TRILL switches use BFD to notice a failed neighbor in far less time than IS-IS Hellos allow.

tldr.problem: TRILL IS-IS Hellos detect a failed neighbor using a Holding Time often set to tens of seconds, with a minimum of one second, and cannot detect failures that only affect unicast frames.
tldr.mechanism: BFD Control and BFD Echo frames travel as unicast RBridge Channel frames, with hop count checks against spoofing and a default authentication key derived from the IS-IS shared secret.
tldr.outcome: RBridges get a low-overhead, fast continuity check for the TRILL data plane. The RFC has since been updated by RFC 8564.

today: RFC 7175 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2014 and has been updated by RFC 8564.

sections.title: Why TRILL Needs Faster Failure Detection
sections.content:
Fast convergence is critical in TRILL networks. The TRILL IS-IS Hellos give a basic neighbor check, but detection by missing Hellos depends on a Holding Time that is commonly tens of seconds and can never be expressed below one second. Some applications, such as Voice over IP, want to know about an interruption much sooner.

Physical-layer detection is not always possible, for example when two bridges sit between two RBridges. Some failures also affect unicast frames while multicast frames still pass, and since all IS-IS Hellos are multicast, they cannot reveal that. The Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) protocol from RFC 5880 is a low-overhead way to test continuity. BFD is already a widely deployed OAM mechanism in IP and MPLS networks using UDP and ACH encapsulation, and this RFC defines the encapsulation for TRILL.
sections.eli5: A slow roll call every few seconds can miss that a friend has left. A quick, constant wave catches it right away.

sections.title: BFD over the RBridge Channel
sections.content:
TRILL BFD runs over the RBridge Channel facility from RFC 7178. It supports unicast neighbor BFD Echo and one-hop and multi-hop BFD Control, and works much like BFD over IP in RFC 5881. Asynchronous and demand modes MUST be supported. Echo is optional and only for single-hop sessions. Multi-destination BFD is described as work in progress.

There is at most one TRILL BFD Control session from RBridge RB1 to RBridge RB2 for each RB1 TRILL port, bound to that interface. Both sides MUST take the Active role, sending initial packets with a zero Your Discriminator. Over a link aggregation that presents one logical interface, only one session can be set up.

TRILL BFD checks the TRILL data plane and sits above whatever link technology is used, such as a pseudowire, Ethernet or PPP. Link-level OAM, and coordination with it, is out of scope.
sections.eli5: Each neighbor pair has exactly one waving game per cable. Both start by waving first, so neither waits for the other.

sections.title: BFD Control Frames
sections.content:
BFD Control frames are unicast RBridge Channel frames, with the protocol-specific data as in Section 4.1 of RFC 5880. One-hop control is typically used to detect link and RBridge failures quickly, so such frames SHOULD be sent at high priority: Inner.VLAN priority 7, queued as maximum priority, and priority 7 in the Outer.VLAN tag if one is added.

An RBridge sends one-hop Control frames to a neighbor only when TRILL IS-IS has seen bidirectional connectivity (the adjacency is in 2-Way or Report state) and both sides advertise BFD as enabled using the BFD-Enabled TLV.

Received Control frames SHOULD be tested before generic BFD processing. A frame with a nonzero M bit in the TRILL Header is discarded, because forged multi-destination frames would make denial-of-service easier. With the MH flag at zero, the hop count must be 0x3F (0x3E if already decremented). With MH at one, it must not be below a configurable value that defaults to 0x30.
sections.eli5: The wave signal gets the fast lane. A wave only counts if it arrived from the right distance, so a stranger far away cannot fake being your neighbor.

sections.title: BFD Echo Frames
sections.content:
A BFD Echo frame is a unicast RBridge Channel frame whose ingress and egress nicknames are both the originator's. A neighbor sends it back through normal TRILL Data forwarding. RBridges whose micro-loop suppression stops them sending a frame back out the port it came in cannot support Echo.

Echo frames SHOULD be sent only when a BFD Control session is established, the neighbor indicates Echo support, the adjacency is in Report state and the originator wants the optional feature. Otherwise the frame uses bandwidth and CPU but is unlikely to return.

The data area is opaque to everyone but the originator, but the RFC suggests including the System IDs of both RBridges, a session identifier, a sequence count and a Message Authentication Code. Returned frames MUST be checked: a nonzero M bit means discard, the hop count must be 0x3E (0x3D if decremented), and the MH bit MUST be one.
sections.eli5: Echo is like shouting into a canyon and listening for your own voice to come back. If it does, the path works.

sections.title: Management and Operations
sections.content:
TRILL BFD parameters are configurable, and the defaults match IP BFD in RFC 5881 except where this document differs, as with hop count. The operator must choose transmission rates that avoid congestion of links, I/O or CPU and avoid false failure detection.

The RFC quotes RFC 5880: an aggressive session with a 50 millisecond detection time, using a 16.7 millisecond transmit interval and a detect multiplier of 3, generates 60 packets per second, around 48 kilobits per second in each direction.
sections.eli5: Waving too fast wastes effort and can cause false alarms, so the person in charge picks a sensible pace.

sections.title: Default Authentication
sections.content:
If IS-IS authentication is not in effect between neighbors, TRILL BFD between them is unsecured by default. If it is, then Control frames MUST by default use BFD Meticulous Keyed SHA1 authentication, with keys derived from the IS-IS shared secret. The derivation is HMAC-SHA256("TRILL BFD Control" | originPortID | originSysID, IS-IS-shared-key), using a 17-byte ASCII string, the 2-byte Port ID and the 6-byte System ID. Port and System IDs are included to limit how much one key is exposed. Other keys or modes MAY be configured.

In the Authentication Section, Auth Type is 5 and Auth Len is 28. Echo authentication is a local matter because the sender checks returned frames, but the RFC suggests different keying material for it, such as the same construction with "TRILL BFD Echo".
sections.eli5: A secret handshake is built from the secret the neighbors already share, so no new password setup is needed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
BFD over TRILL is generally analogous to BFD over IP. Its authentication facility can protect BFD payloads, but no encryption or other security features exist at the BFD-over-TRILL level. For more, the RFC points to RFC 5881 for BFD, RFC 7178 for the RBridge Channel and RFC 6325 for TRILL. The hop count and M bit checks in Section 3.2 address spoofing and denial-of-service concerns.

IANA allocated two RBridge Channel protocol numbers: 0x002 for BFD Control and 0x003 for BFD Echo.
sections.eli5: The secret handshake proves who is waving but does not hide the wave, and the distance checks block most fakes.

cells: Not less than 0x30 by default, configurable
